Arrays

What is an array?
An array is a single variable that can hold multiple values (a collection). In Bash, arrays are indexed (numeric indices starting from 0) or
associative (string keys, Bash 4+).
● Indexed arrays: arr=(a b c)
● Associative arrays: declare -A map (Bash 4+)
Note: Arrays are a Bash feature. Portable /bin/sh scripts typically do not support arrays.
Why use arrays?
● Store lists (filenames, user names, numbers) in one variable.
● Easier iteration and batch processing.
● Better structure than many separate scalar variables.

Creating (declaring) arrays
1. Explicit assignment (preferred shorthand)
# Create an indexed array with four elements
arr=(apple banana cherry "fruit salad")
1. Assign element-by-element
# Put value into index 0
arr[0]=apple
arr[1]=banana
arr[5]=grape
1. Declare an empty array and append later
declare -a list # optional: declare as an indexed array (for clarity)
list=() # empty array
list+=(one) # append 'one'
list+=(two three)
1. Create array from command output
arr=(red green blue)
echo "\${arr[0]}" # prints 'red'
echo ${arr[@]} # word-splits and expands each element
echo "\${arr[@]}" # each element preserved as a single word
echo "\${arr[*]}" # joins elements with first character of IFS (default space)

Useful array properties and operations
arr=(10 20 30 40)
echo "Length = ${#arr[@]}" # prints 4
echo "Indices = ${!arr[@]}" # prints "0 1 2 3"

arr+=(50)
arr[1]=99

Unix Programming with Standard
Input and Output

Introduction to Standard Streams
• In Unix systems, communication between
applications is achieved using standard streams:
• • stdin – Standard Input Stream
• • stdout – Standard Output Stream
• • stderr – Standard Error Stream
• These streams act as communication channels
between programs and the terminal.

Input/Output Streams Example
• Example: Using grep with input redirection
• #!/usr/bin/env bash
• echo pattern | grep pattern
• • 'echo pattern' sends output to grep via
stdin.
• • grep outputs matching results to stdout.
• The script running at the console:

Error Stream Example
• stderr is used for reporting errors independently
from stdout.
• Example:
• ls > /tmp/log
• ls /not/existed_path > /tmp/log
• • Errors are displayed on console because they
use stderr.

Redirecting Streams
It is possible to manipulate the standard streams: redirect
them or use pipes to process them.
• Streams can be redirected or piped:
• '>' redirects stdout to a file.
• '2>' redirects stderr.
• '/dev/null' discards unwanted output.
• Example:
• ls /not/existed_path 2> /dev/null
Redirecting Streams

Discarding Output
In some cases, it is useful to drop all of the
application output (to save storage space or
remove the unimportant sources of data to
analyze). We should remember that we should
mute not just the standard output stream but
the standard error stream also. Let's look at an
example of how does it work.
Discarding Output

• In both lines of script standard output stream redirected to
file /dev/null. This file is not a file itself: but a special Linux
device with a file interface. It has a write function available from
shell (that does nothing). So all of the input is just dropped. But the
second string of the script has a difference from the first one:
"2>&1" at the end of the command. These symbols tell that the
second standard stream ( standard error stream ) needs to be
directed at the first standard stream (standard output stream)
permanently for this command. That is why we see only one error
message displayed in the console - at the second command string
of the script standard error stream redirected to terminating file
device /dev/null in the end.

Pipelined Streams
• It also can be useful to modify the stream. is
able to run several applications connected by
the streams.

• The script running at the console:
Here we collect the listing and set “ls” standard output stream as grep
standard input stream by using “|”. On “2>” standard errors stream is
redirected to the termination file. The output stream of grep contains
the "/tmp/a" filename from listing that matches by grep pattern.

Conclusion
• • Unix uses three main data streams for
process communication.
• • Streams can be redirected, piped, or
discarded as needed.
• • Mastering stdin, stdout, and stderr is
essential for shell scripting.

Linux Commands
LINUX COMMANDS

Linux Commands
UNIX Commands
• A command is a program which interacts with the
kernel to provide the environment and perform the
functions called for by the user.
• A command can be: a built-in shell command; an
executable shell file, known as a shell script; or a
source compiled, object code file.
• The shell is a command line interpreter. The user
interacts with the kernel through the shell. You can
write ASCII (text) scripts to be acted upon by a
shell.

Linux Commands
UNIX Shell
• The shell sits between you and the operating
system, acting as a command interpreter.
• It reads your terminal input and translates the
commands into actions taken by the system. The
shell is analogous to command.com in DOS.
• When you log into the system you are given a
default shell.
• When the shell starts up it reads its startup files
and may set environment variables, command
search paths, and command aliases, and executes
any commands specified in these files.

Linux Commands
UNIX Shell
•The original shell was the Bourne shell, sh.
•Every Unix platform will either have the Bourne shell,
or a Bourne compatible shell available.
• The default prompt for the Bourne shell is $ (or #, for
the root user).
• Another popular shell is C Shell. The default prompt
for the C shell is %.

Linux Commands

Superblock
A superblock is a special data structure that holds information about the entire file system.
It’s like the table of contents for the disk — the OS uses it to understand how to read and manage files.
● The OS cannot use the file system if the superblock is missing or corrupted.
ext2/ext4 keep backup copies of the superblock in different places so that if one is damaged, it can be restored.
In memory: struct super_block in the kernel represents a mounted file system.
On disk: Contains permanent info about the file system.
Key fields in struct super_block:
● s_dev → Device identifier
● s_blocksize → Block size in bytes
● s_flags → File system state (read-only, dirty, etc.)
● s_type → File system type (ext2, procfs, etc.)
● s_mounted → Pointer to root inode
● s_op → Pointer to superblock operations (functions for mounting, unmounting, syncing, etc.)

Locking/Unlocking superblock
●
In a multitasking OS like UNIX, multiple processes (or threads inside the kernel) might try to read or
modify the same superblock at the same time.
●
If two things change it at once, data can become corrupted.
●
Locking ensures that only one process can access/modify the superblock at a time.
●
WORKING:
The kernel uses a flag inside struct super_block (e.g., s_lock) to mark whether it’s in use.
Locking:
● If s_lock is already set → another process is using it → wait until it’s free.
● If not set → set it to 1 and proceed.
Unlocking:
● Set s_lock back to 0.
● Wake up any processes waiting to use it.

PROC FILE SYSTEM
● procfs is a virtual file system — it doesn’t store files on a disk.
● Instead, it’s a way for the kernel to expose information about running processes and system
status as files.
● Usually mounted at /proc.
Structure
● /proc/<PID>/ → Directory for each running process (PID = Process ID).
○ Contains files like:
■ cmdline → Command that started the process
■ status → Process state and memory usage
■ fd/ → File descriptors used by the process
● System-wide info:
○ /proc/cpuinfo → CPU details
○ /proc/meminfo → Memory usage
○ /proc/uptime → How long the system has been running
●

● Every process has a directory in /proc/pid which contains files relevant
to the process.
How procfs Works Internally
● Mounted during system startup by the kernel.
● In VFS terms:
1. VFS calls read_super() when mounting /proc.
2. proc_read_super() sets up the proc file system’s superblock
in memory.
3. Root inode of /proc is created.
● Files and directories in /proc are generated on the fly when you
open/read them — nothing is stored permanently.

Originally used MINIX file system.Serious limitations like partition
●
size,file name size etc.Proposed ext file system which was even
worse.Led to excessive fragmentation.Remy Card et’al propose ext2fs
which is the Unix file system.
Influenced by BSD FFS.Every partition is divided into a number of block
●
groups,corresponding to the cylinder groups of FFS,with each block
group holding a copy of superblock,inode and data blocks.

STRUCTURE OF E2FS
●
ext2 = Second Extended File System, a classic Linux file system.
●
It replaced the older MINIX and ext file systems, which had size and performance limits.
●
Still used today in some cases, and its design influenced ext3 and ext4.
Instead of keeping all inodes in one big table and all data blocks in another far away, ext2 divides the disk into
block groups.
Why?
● Keeps related data close together → reduces disk head movement → faster.
● Balances file placement to avoid fragmentation.
Each block group contains:
1. Superblock copy (for backup)
2. Block group descriptor (info about this group)
3. Block bitmap → Tracks free/used data blocks
4. Inode bitmap → Tracks free/used inodes
5. Inode table → Metadata for files in this group
6. Data blocks → The actual file contents
●

Directories in ext2
● In ext2, a directory is just a special file.
● Instead of storing text or images, its data blocks contain a list of directory entries.
2. Directory Entry Structure
Each directory entry has:
struct ext2_dir_entry {
unsigned long inode; // Inode number of the file
unsigned short rec_len; // Size of this directory entry
unsigned short name_len; // Length of the file name
char name[EXT2_NAME_LEN]; // The file name itself
};
● inode → Points to the file’s metadata
● rec_len → Lets the OS know where the next entry starts
● name_len → Length of the file name
● name → Actual file name

Directories in e2fs
What happens on a delete?
ext2 doesn’t shuffle entries around when you delete a file.
Instead:
1. The inode number is set to 0.
2. The previous entry’s rec_len is updated to cover the empty space.
Why?
● Avoids unnecessary moving of data.
● The space can be reused later.

Block allocation in e2fs
What is Block Allocation?
● When you create or grow a file, the file system must decide which disk blocks to use to store
the file’s data.
● Good allocation = faster file access, less fragmentation.
ext2’s Allocation Goals
● Prevent fragmentation (scattering file pieces all over the disk).
● Keep related data close together for speed.
Target-Oriented Allocation
When ext2 needs a block:
1. First → Look for free space right next to the last block of the file.
2. If not available → Look for a free block within 32 blocks of the last one.
3. If still not found → Use a free block in the same block group.
4. As a last resort → Allocate from another block group.
●

Pre-allocation (Clustering)
● When ext2 allocates a block, it can reserve up to 8 following blocks if they’re free.
● If the file is closed before all reserved blocks are used → the extra blocks are
released.
● This improves performance for sequential writes.
How ext2 Decides the Target Block
● Let:
○ n = logical block number needed
○ l = last allocated block number
● Target = l + 1 (next block in sequence) if possible.

What are STDIN, STDOUT, STDERR?
• These are standard data streams in Unix/Linux used for input
and output.
STDIN (Standard Input) – File descriptor 0
STDOUT (Standard Output) – File descriptor 1
STDERR (Standard Error) – File descriptor 2

STDIN (Standard Input)
Default input source, typically the keyboard.
File descriptor: 0
Used in commands to receive input from user or file.
Example: sort < names.txt

STDOUT (Standard Output)
Default output destination, typically the terminal.
File descriptor: 1
Used to send results of commands.
Example: ls > files.txt

STDERR (Standard Error)
Used for outputting error messages.
File descriptor: 2
By default, goes to the terminal like STDOUT.
Example: cat nofile.txt 2> error.txt

Redirection Examples
1. Redirect STDOUT to a file: command > output.txt
ls > files.txt
This will save the list of files into files.txt instead of displaying it on the screen.
2. Redirect STDERR to a file: command 2> error.txt
cat nofile.txt 2> error.txt
This saves the "No such file or directory" error to error.txt.
3. Redirect both STDOUT and STDERR: command > all.txt 2>&1
ls existing.txt missing.txt > all.txt 2>&1
This command will list existing.txt, and if missing.txt doesn’t exist, the error
will also go into all.txt.
4. Discard errors: command 2>/dev/null
cat file.txt 2>/dev/null
Errors (if any) like "file not found" won't appear on the screen.

What is a Pipe?
• Pipes (`|`) pass output of one command as
input to another.
• Build powerful command chains without temp
files.

Syntax & How Pipes Work
• command1 | command2
• STDOUT of command1 becomes STDIN for
command2.

Examples of Pipes
• ls | sort – List and sort files
• cat file.txt | wc -l – Count lines
• ps -ef | grep bash – Filter processes
• ls -l | tee output.txt – Show & save output

Multiple Pipes
• cat file | sort | uniq | wc -l
• Combines filters for complex tasks.

Examples
Example 1: Search for a pattern and count lines
cat file.txt | grep "error" | wc -l
Counts how many lines contain the word “error”.
Example 2: Sort and remove duplicate lines

who | cut -d' ' -f1 | sort | uniq
Example 4: Count number of words in a file
cat file.txt | wc –w

ifconfig | grep "inet " | awk '{print $2}'

Q5. Based on closest Pair in 1 D.
Since every train takes exactly T hours:
Arrival Time=Departure Time+T
So, minimizing difference in arrival times is equivalent to minimizing:
∣Departure_i − Departure_j|
Thus, the problem reduces to:
Find two departure times with minimum absolute difference.
This is a classic Closest Pair in 1D problem.
Algorithm Idea
1. Sort the departure times
2. Divide the array into two halves
3. Recursively find minimum difference in:
o Left half
o Right half
4. Also check the minimum difference across the boundary
5. Return the minimum of all three
Algorithm Steps [3 marks]
Let D[1…n] be departure times.
Step 1: Sort
Sort D in increasing order
Step 2: Recursive Function
MinDiff(D, low, high):
if high - low <= 1:
return |D[high] - D[low]|
mid = (low + high) / 2
leftMin = MinDiff(D, low, mid)
rightMin = MinDiff(D, mid+1, high)
crossMin = |D[mid+1] - D[mid]|
return min(leftMin, rightMin, crossMin)

Example [1 mark]
Departure times:
[1, 5, 9, 12, 13, 20]
After sorting:
[1, 5, 9, 12, 13, 20]
Differences:
4, 4, 3, 1, 7
Minimum difference = 1 hour
So family waits only 1 hour difference at destination.
Time Complexity Analysis
Sorting:
O(nlogn)
Recurrence Relation:
T(n)=2T(n/2)+O(1) [ 0.5 mark]
Using Master Theorem:
T(n)=O(n)
Overall Complexity:
O(nlogn) [ 0.5 mark]

Answer 1: Android Software Stack Architecture (2_marks)
The Android architecture consists of five major layers, arranged from bottom to top as
shown below:
Applications
Application Framework
Android Runtime (ART)
Native Libraries
Linux Kernel
1. Linux Kernel
The Linux Kernel forms the foundation of the Android operating system.
It is responsible for:
• Process management
• Memory management
• Device drivers (camera, display, audio, Bluetooth, Wi-Fi)
• Power management
• Security (SELinux)
All Android applications run on top of the Linux kernel, which abstracts the underlying
hardware and provides core system services.
2. Native Libraries
This layer contains C/C++ libraries that provide core functionalities required by the Android
system, such as:
• SQLite (database support)
• OpenGL ES (graphics rendering)
• WebKit (browser engine)
• Media framework (audio and video playback)
These libraries are accessed by higher layers through the Android Runtime and Framework.
3. Android Runtime (ART)
The Android Runtime provides:
• Core Java libraries
• Execution environment for Android applications

Each Android app runs in its own process with its own instance of ART, ensuring isolation
and security. ART converts bytecode into native instructions and manages garbage collection,
memory allocation, and performance optimization.
4. Application Framework
The Application Framework exposes high-level APIs to developers and manages application
components.
Key components include:
• Activity Manager
• Window Manager
• Content Providers
• Resource Manager
• Notification Manager
This layer allows developers to reuse system components and interact with system services
without directly accessing low-level code.
5. Applications
The topmost layer consists of user-installed and system applications, such as:
• Phone
• Contacts
• Browser
• Messaging apps
These applications are written primarily in Java/Kotlin and use the APIs provided by the
Application Framework.
Interaction During Application Execution
When an Android app is launched:
1. The Application Framework requests resources and system services.
2. Requests are handled by ART and native libraries.
3. Hardware access is managed through the Linux Kernel.
4. Results are passed back up the stack to the application.
This layered interaction ensures efficiency, security, and abstraction.

Android Activity Lifecycle (2_marks)
An Activity represents a single screen in an Android application. The Activity Lifecycle
defines the states an activity goes through from creation to destruction.
Common Lifecycle States
• onCreate() – Activity is created
• onStart() – Activity becomes visible
• onResume() – Activity comes to foreground and is interactive
• onPause() – Activity partially visible
• onStop() – Activity no longer visible
• onDestroy() – Activity destroyed
Transition from onPause() to onStop()
When an activity transitions from onPause() to onStop(), the following occurs:
onPause()
• Triggered when the activity is partially visible
• Used to:
o Pause animations
o Save lightweight UI state
o Commit unsaved changes
The system expects onPause() to execute quickly to allow smooth transitions.
onStop()
• Triggered when the activity is completely hidden
• Used to:
o Release heavy resources (camera, sensors, receivers)
o Stop background tasks
o Save persistent data
After onStop(), the activity may:
• Be restarted (onRestart())
• Be destroyed (onDestroy())

• When DisplayActivity is launched, RegistrationActivity may enter onPause() →

Q3. What is a Spinner in Android? How does it differ from a RadioGroup? In what situation would a Spinner be a more appropriate UI choice? [Apply Level (CO2) 2 Marks] Solution: A Spinner in Android is a drop-down UI component that allows users to select one item from a list of options. When the user taps the spinner, a list appears from which a single item can be chosen. Difference from RadioGroup: • Spinner: Displays options in a drop-down menu, saving screen space. • RadioGroup: Displays all options as visible radio buttons, allowing the user to select only one. When Spinner is better: A Spinner is preferred when there are many options or when screen space is limited, such as selecting a country, language, or category. Q4. role of an Adapter in connecting a ListView or GridView to its data source in Android. Name two types of adapters built into Android and state when each is appropriate to use. [Apply Level (CO2) 2 Marks] Solution: An Adapter in Android acts as a bridge between the data source and UI components such as ListView or GridView. It retrieves data from a source (such as an array, database, or ArrayList) and converts each data item into a View that can be displayed in the list or grid. Two Built-in Android Adapters 1. ArrayAdapter o Used when the data source is a simple array or ArrayList of items. o Suitable for displaying a single text item per row in components like ListView or Spinner. 2. SimpleAdapter o Used when data contains multiple fields (e.g., text and images) mapped to multiple views in a layout. o Suitable for custom list items with multiple UI components. Thus, ArrayAdapter is ideal for simple lists, while SimpleAdapter is used for more structured data requiring multiple views per item.

Solution: a) Difference between Explicit Intent and Implicit Intent (2 Marks) An Explicit Intent is used to start a specific activity or component by explicitly specifying its class name. It is typically used for communication between activities within the same application. Example: Intent intent = new Intent (MainActivity.this, ResultActivity.class); startActivity(intent); An Implicit Intent does not specify the exact component to start. Instead, it declares a general action to perform, and Android finds a suitable application installed on the device that can handle the request. Example from the Scenario • Sharing the quiz result message • Calling the hotline number • Opening a web page in the browser All of these actions involve external applications, so Implicit Intents are used. Why Explicit Intent Should NOT Be Used Explicit Intents should not be used because: • The app does not know which specific external application (WhatsApp, Gmail, SMS, etc.) the user wants to use for sharing. • Dialer and browser applications vary across devices and manufacturers.

Android Architecture & Manifest File Q1(a): Android Architecture vs Linux Distribution - ART & HAL Android's architecture differs fundamentally from a traditional Linux distribution in how it optimizes for mobile-constrained environments: Android Runtime (ART): • ART uses Ahead-of-Time (AOT) compilation: app bytecode (DEX) is compiled to native machine code at install time. • Unlike Java's JVM which uses Just-in-Time (JIT) at runtime, ART eliminates runtime compilation overhead - apps start faster and execute efficiently. • ART also uses Profile-Guided Compilation (PGC) - it identifies hot code paths and compiles only those, reducing storage and memory use. • Garbage Collection in ART is concurrent and compacting, reducing GC pauses significantly vs older Dalvik VM. • Traditional Linux runs native ELF binaries directly, Android adds the ART layer to safely sandbox app code in a managed environment. Hardware Abstraction Layer (HAL): • HAL acts as a bridge between Android's framework and device-specific hardware drivers. • In standard Linux, apps interact directly with kernel drivers (via /dev). Hardware Abstraction Layer (HAL): • HAL acts as a bridge between Android's framework and device-specific hardware drivers. • In standard Linux, apps interact directly with kernel drivers (via /dev). Android instead defines standardized HAL interfaces (e.g., camera.h, sensors.h). • OEMs implement HAL for their specific hardware, the framework calls HAL APIs - this decouples hardware specifics from the OS framework. • Since Android 8.0 (Treble), HAL runs in isolated processes (HIDL/AIDL), so a HAL crash does not crash the system server - improving stability on constrained devices. • This also allows Android to receive framework OTA updates without requiring new hardware drivers from OEMs. In summary: ART optimizes CPU and memory usage at the app execution level, HAL decouples hardware variability at the driver level - together they make Android run efficiently across a wide range of mobile hardware. SQLite, Content Providers & Threading Q3(a): Content Provider vs Shared SQLite File - Security & Architecture Security Implications: • Shared SQLite file: Storing the database in a world-readable or shared location (e.g., external storage) exposes it to any app with READ_EXTERNAL_STORAGE permission. Even internal storage sharing via file permissions bypasses Android's app sandbox - all three external apps can read/write the raw DB file, risking data corruption and unauthorized modification. • Content Provider: Acts as a controlled API over your database. The provider's app runs in its own process, external apps never access the raw file. You grant read/write URIs selectively via android:readPermission and android:writePermission in Manifest. External apps can only perform what the provider exposes - no direct table access. Architectural Implications: • A Content Provider enforces a defined contract (URI scheme, column names) - changes to internal schema don't break external apps as long as the URI contract is maintained. • A shared file requires all three apps

access. Architectural Implications: • A Content Provider enforces a defined contract (URI scheme, column names) - changes to internal schema don't break external apps as long as the URI contract is maintained. • A shared file requires all three apps to know and agree on the exact schema - tightly coupled. • Providers support per-URI permissions, allowing temporary access grants via grantUriPermission(). When to use FileProvider over SQLiteOpenHelper: • Use FileProvider when you need to share a file (not structured data) with another app - e.g., sharing a photo/PDF via an Intent with ACTION_SEND. • FileProvider (a subclass of ContentProvider) generates content:// URIs for files in your private storage, allowing temporary, controlled sharing without exposing file paths. • Use SQLiteOpenHelper (directly or behind a ContentProvider) for structured relational data that needs querying, filtering, and joining. • FileProvider is the right choice when another app needs to VIEW or RECEIVE a file (camera photo, PDF report), not query rows from a database. Role of startActivityForResult in this context:
• startActivityForResult(intent, requestCode) launches DetailActivity while keeping MainActivity alive in
the back stack.
• When DetailActivity calls setResult(RESULT_OK, data) + finish(), control returns to MainActivity's
onActivityResult() callback.
• This allows MainActivity to receive a result payload (the deleted student's ID) and immediately refresh the
RecyclerView - ensuring the list reflects the current database state without a full Activity restart.
• This is the classic two-Activity communication pattern: Parent launches Child with startActivityForResult,
Child signals completion with setResult, Parent handles in onActivityResult.
• Note: In modern Android development, ActivityResultLauncher (registerForActivityResult) is the
recommended replacement for the deprecated startActivityForResult, but the pattern and purpose are
identical.

Basic Statistical Concepts
Measures of Central Tendency

Measures of central tendency are also usually 	called as the averages.
They give us an idea about the concentration of  the  values  in  the  central  part  of  the distribution.
The  following  are  the  five  measures  of central tendency that are in common use:
(i) Arithmetic mean, (ii) Median, (iii) Mode,
(iv) Geometric mean, and (v) Harmonic mean
(vi) weighted mean

most commonly
occurring value
The average of the data
The middle of the data

Mean (Average)
Mean locate the centre of distribution. Also known as arithmetic mean
Most Common Measure
The mean is simply the sum of the values divided
by the total number of items in the set.
Affected by Extreme Values

Merits:
It is easy to understand and easy to calculate.
It is based upon all the observations
It is familiar to common man and rigidly defined.
It is capable of further mathematical treatment.

Demerits
It cannot be determined by inspection. Arithmetic mean cannot be used if we are
dealing	with
qualitative which	cannot	be	measured
characteristics, quantitatively
like caste, religion, sex.

Arithmetic	mean	is very	much	affected	by 	extreme values.

Properties arithmetic mean
The sum of deviations of the observations from their arithmetic mean is always zero: [∑(X−X)=0]
[∑(X-X)2 is minimum]: The sum of the square of the deviations of the items from their arithmetic mean is minimum. The sum of the square of the deviations of the items from their arithmetic mean is less than the sum of the square of deviations from any other value.
If each observation of a series is increased or decreased by a constant, then the arithmetic mean of the new series will also get increased or decreased by that constant respectively.

Properties arithmetic mean
If each observation of a series is multiplied or divided by a constant, then the arithmetic mean of the new series will also get multiplied or divided by that constant respectively.
Mean of the Combined Series: If the arithmetic mean of two or more related series is given, then it is possible to calculate the combined arithmetic mean of the series as a whole.
If any two values out of arithmetic mean, number of items, or a total of the values are known, then it is possible to calculate the third value: The missing items, missing frequency, or correct mean can be determined

Geometric Mean
Geometric mean (G.M.) of a set of n observations is the nth root of their product.
G.M. is specially useful in averaging ratios, percentages, and rates of increase between two periods.
For example: G.M. is appropriate average to be used for computing the average rate of growth of population, or average increase in the rate of profit, sales, production etc.,
It is useful in the construction of Index Number.
Geometric Mean

Merits and Demerits of G.M.
Merits:
It is rigidly defined.
It is based on all the observations
Less affected by the extreme values
Not affected much by fluctuations of sampling
Demerits:
Difficult to calculate and difficult to understand
Cannot calculate if value of any observations is zero
Less weightage is given to large items and more to small items.

Harmonic Mean
Harmonic mean (H.M.)is computed by calculating the reciprocal of the arithmetic mean of the reciprocals of the given values of the variable.
In other words, H.M. is the total number of items of a variable divided by the sum of the reciprocals of a variable divided by the sum of the reciprocals of the values of the variable.
It's generally used when dealing with averages of units, like speed or other rates and ratios.
Harmonic Mean

Merits and Demerits of H.M.
Merits:
It is rigidly defined.
It is based on all the observations
Less affected by the extreme values
Better suitable to calculated time, rates, ratio than any other average
Used to measure relative changes.
Demerits:
Difficult to calculate and understand
Not very popular and less frequently used
Cannot be calculated when there are both positive and negative items in a series or when a single or more items are zero.

Median
Measure of Central Tendency.
The median is determined by sorting the data set from lowest to highest values and taking the data point in the middle of the sequence.
Middle Value In Ordered Sequence
If Odd n, Middle Value of Sequence
If Even n, Average of 2 Middle Value
Not Affected by Extreme Values

Merits:
It is rigidly defined
It	is easy 	to	understand	and	easy	to calculate.
It is not at all affected by extreme values.
It can be calculated for distributions	with open-end classes.
Median	is the only average 	to	be used while dealing with qualitative data.

Demerits:
In	case	of	even	number	of	observations 	median cannot be determined exactly.
It is not based on all the observations.
It	is	not capable	of further	mathematical treatment

The mode is the most frequently occurring value in the data set.
If in a series two items occur more frequently such a series is known as bimodal.

Abuses of Regression Regression is widely used and frequently misused; several common abuses of regression are briefly mentioned here. Care should be taken in selecting variables with which to construct regression equations and in determining the form of the model. It is possible to develop sta- tistically significant relationships among variables that are completely unrelated in a causal sense. For example, we might attempt to relate the shear strength of spot welds with the num- ber of empty parking spaces in the visitor parking lot. A straight line may even appear to pro- vide a good fit to the data, but the relationship is an unreasonable one on which to rely. You can’t increase the weld strength by blocking

spaces in the visitor parking lot. A straight line may even appear to pro- vide a good fit to the data, but the relationship is an unreasonable one on which to rely. You can’t increase the weld strength by blocking off parking spaces. A strong observed association between variables does not necessarily imply that a causal relationship exists between those variables. This type of effect is encountered fairly often in retrospective data analysis, and even in observational studies. Designed experiments are the only way to determine cause- and-effect relationships. Correlation Analysis

Introduction
Correlation and regression are statistical techniques used to examine relationships between variables.
Correlation measures the strength and direction of association.
Regression estimates the functional relationship and predicts one variable using another.

Types of Correlation
Positive correlation: variables move in the same direction.
Negative correlation: variables move in opposite directions.
Zero correlation: no linear relationship.

Scatter Diagram
A graphical method used to visualize the relationship between two variables.
Upward pattern → positive correlation
Downward pattern → negative correlation

a. Strong positive correlation between x and y. The points lie close to a straight line with y increasing as x increases.
b. Weak, positive correlation between x and y. The trend shown is that y increases as x increases but the points are not close to a straight line
c. No correlation between x and y; the points are distributed randomly on the graph.
d. Weak, negative correlation between x and y. The trend shown is that y decreases as x increases but the points do not lie close to a straight line
e. Strong, negative correlation. The points lie close to a straight line, with y decreasing as x increases

Correlation can have a value:
1 is a perfect positive correlation
0 is no correlation (the values don't seem linked at all)
-1 is a perfect negative correlation

In statistics, there are three types of correlations:
Pearson correlation
Kendall rank correlation
Spearman correlation

Assumptions of Correlation
The variables considered in correlation analysis should be independent.
The observations should be randomly selected from the population.
The variables are generally assumed to follow a normal distribution.
The relationship between the variables should be linear.
The data should exhibit homoscedasticity, meaning equal variance across observations.

Presence of outliers can distort the value and interpretation of the correlation coefficient.
A scatterplot helps visualize the direction and possible relationship between variables.
Correlation coefficients measure the degree of relationship between variables.
Correlation analysis identifies association but does not establish causation

Spearman rank correlation is a non-parametric test that is used to measure the degree of association between two variables.
It was developed by Spearman, thus it is called the Spearman rank correlation.
Spearman rank correlation test does not assume any assumptions about the distribution of the data and is the appropriate correlation analysis when the variables are measured on a scale that is at least ordinal.

UNIT 3 Regression Analysis 3.1. Definition Regression analysis is one of the most commonly used statistical techniques in social and behavioral sciences as well as in physical sciences which involves identifying and evaluating the relationship between a dependent variable and one or more independent variables, which are also called predictor or explanatory variables. It is particularly useful for assess and adjusting for confounding. Model of the relationship is hypothesized and estimates of the parameter values are used to develop an estimated regression equation. Various tests are then employed to determine if the model is satisfactory. If the model is deemed satisfactory, the estimated regression equation can be used to predict the value of the dependent variable given values for the independent variables. Linear regression explores relationships that can be readily described by straight lines or their generalization to many dimensions. A surprisingly large number of problems can be solved by linear regression, and even more by means of transformation of the original variables that result in linear relationships among the transformed variables. When there is a single continuous dependent variable and a single independent variable, the analysis is called a simple linear regression analysis. This analysis assumes that there is

the original variables that result in linear relationships among the transformed variables. When there is a single continuous dependent variable and a single independent variable, the analysis is called a simple linear regression analysis. This analysis assumes that there is a linear association between the two variables. Multiple regression is to learn more about the relationship between several independent or predictor variables and a dependent or criterion variable. Independent variables are characteristics that can be measured directly; these variables are also called predictor or explanatory variables used to predict or to explain the behavior of the dependent variable. Dependent variable is a characteristic whose value depends on the values of independent variables. Reliability and Validity: • Does the model make intuitive sense? Is the model easy to understand and interpret? • Are all coefficients statistically significant? (p-values less than .05) • Are the signs associated with the coefficients as expected? • Does the model predict values that are reasonably close to the actual values? • Is the model sufficiently sound? (High R-square, low standard error, etc.) 3.2. The primary objective of regression is to develop a linear relationship between a response variable and explanatory variables for the purposes of prediction, assumes that a functional linear relationship exists, and alternative approaches (functional regression) are superior. 3.3. Assumption of Regression Analysis The regression model is based on the following assumptions.  The relationship between independent variable and dependent is linear.  The expected value of the error term is zero  The variance of the error term is constant for all the values of the independent variable, the assumption of homoscedasticity.  There is no autocorrelation.  The independent variable is uncorrelated with the error term.  The error term is normally distributed.  On an average difference between the observed value (yi) and the predicted value (ˆyi) is zero.  On an average the estimated values of errors and values of independent variables are not related to each other.  The squared differences between the observed value and the predicted value are similar.  There is some variation in independent variable. T1 Solution Solution 1: [2 marks for identifying the correct software process model and 2 marks for justifying why this model outperforms] The Spiral Model is the most suitable software process model for this case. It emphasises continuous risk analysis, which helps address security vulnerabilities and regulatory changes early in each iteration. Unlike the Waterfall model, it allows redesign of core modules without restarting the entire process. Compared to Agile, the Spiral model provides stronger documentation and control, which is critical for investor oversight and regulatory compliance. Its iterative cycles also support coordination among distributed teams while keeping budget and risks under control. Q2. Cohesion: The BookManager module shows Low Cohesion (Coincidental Cohesion)
because it performs several unrelated tasks, such as adding books, generating reports, and
sending notifications, within the same module. These functions are not strongly related to a
single responsibility.
● Coupling: The IssueBook module directly accesses the internal data of the BookManager
module, which indicates Content Coupling. This type of coupling is very strong and
undesirable because one module depends on the internal implementation of another module.
● Justification: Due to low cohesion and high coupling, a small modification in the
BookManager module affects multiple modules in the system, making maintenance difficult.

def process_marks(marks):

a) Identify issues in the above code based on coding standards (readability, efficiency, error

b) Explain how code review and code walkthrough processes can help improve the quality,
readability, and maintainability of this code.
Solution: a) Issues in the Code Based on Coding Standards
1. Readability Issues
• Use of range(len(marks)) makes the code less readable; direct iteration is preferred.
• Variable name i is not descriptive.
• Function name process_marks is vague and does not clearly indicate its purpose.
• No comments or documentation are provided.
2. Efficiency Issues
• Using indexing (marks[i]) instead of direct iteration is less efficient.
• Built-in functions like sum() are not used, which are more optimized.
3. Error Handling Issues
• No check for an empty list → may cause division by zero error.
• No validation of input (e.g., non-numeric values in the list).
• Assumes input is always valid.
4. Maintainability Issues
• Passing condition (avg >= 50) is hardcoded instead of configurable.
• Code is not modular or reusable.
B) Role of Code Review and Code Walkthrough
Code Review

• A formal process where peers examine the code. • Helps detect errors such as division by zero. • Suggests improvements like using sum() and better variable names. • Ensures coding standards and best practices are followed. • Improves maintainability and overall code quality. Code Walkthrough • An informal process where the developer explains the code to others. • Helps identify logical mistakes during explanation. • Promotes better understanding among team members. • Encourages suggestions for improving readability and structure.
